Lessons.Title: Same Perimeter, Different Shapes
ExplanationParagraphs: First Edition 2021 G3 U07 Lesson 7 original teacher lesson, preparation and all four student PDF pages were inspected on the authorized PC. The 10 original figures A–J were independently checked at the vector-path level in the original student-task PDF, including concave perimeters. The picture itself is not embedded. Original gated publisher Cool-down Create Your Own Shapes is not available; a separate first-party Edulytics Cool-down is not represented as its reproduction.

Goals: find the perimeters of two-dimensional shapes and explain that very different polygon outlines may have equal perimeter. Standards 3.MD.D.8 and warm-up 3.NBT.A.2. Source structure: True/False four multi-digit addition identities (10 min), All Kinds of Shapes (15 min), Draw Your Own (20 min), synthesis (10 min), gated publisher Cool-down (5 min). Original teacher uses MLR7 Compare and Connect, partner dialogue, and multiple counting/addition strategies.

Warm-up starts with four TRUE or FALSE equality judgments for 123+75+123+75. That sum is 396. Expanding into 100+100+70+70+5+5+3+3 yields 356, so statement 1 is FALSE; regrouping as 2×123+2×75 gives 396 so statement 2 is TRUE; 208+208=416 so statement 3 FALSE; and 246+150=396 so statement 4 TRUE. Explain why the regrouping is valid without separately adding the same expression repeatedly.

Activity 1 original student PDF page 2 contains exactly TEN labelled dot-grid polygons A–J. The normalized side interval geometry was extracted from the source PDF vector paths (one grid side = 19.36 PDF points). The verified perimeters are: A 18, B 16, C 10, D 10, E 16, F 22, G 18, H 18, I 10, J 22 grid units. Source teacher independently confirms A and G have the SAME perimeter even though their geometry looks different.

All same-perimeter families: 18 units = A,G,H; 16 units = B,E; 10 units = C,D,I; 22 units = F,J. These are inclusive groups derived from all source ten original shapes; the actual public activity asks pupils to choose ANY THREE, find their perimeters and identify one OTHER shape with an equal perimeter. The Edulytics practice has a separately anchored check available for each source figure so students can choose rather than being forced to solve all ten.

Perimeter is the total length around an outline, measured using equally spaced horizontal and vertical dot-to-dot intervals. A has two upward one-unit step projections; F and J are concave polygons; I has an inside corner. Count the continuous boundary once, including every indentation. For a 4×4 square B the perimeter is 16; for a 7×1 rectangle E the perimeter is also 16, despite their different area. A polygon with 6×3 sides H gives 18, the same as 7×2 G and stepped A. Equal perimeter never implies equal area or congruence.

Activity 2 original student PDF pages 3–4 asks for TWO DISTINCT shapes for EACH target perimeter 12, 26 and 48 units, then allows partners to CHOOSE a target perimeter and draw their own shape. The source teacher explicitly restricts shapes to horizontal and vertical dot-grid segments because a diagonal joining grid dots is NOT one grid-unit length. For each target, learners must present two different valid shapes and show a perimeter sum: e.g. 1×5 and 2×4 rectangles each have perimeter 12; 1×12 and 2×11 each 26; 1×23 and 2×22 each 48, subject to the physical dot-grid dimensions. Teachers may accept many nonrectangular valid shapes and inspect diagrams, not just typed counts.

The source grids for 12 units, 26 units and 48 units have visibly different available drawing spaces. A theoretical 1×23 rectangle cannot be drawn on a grid shorter than 23 intervals; students need feasible dimensions on their actual printed grid. Better examples that fit the source spaces: 1×5 vs 2×4 for 12, 3×10 vs 4×9 for 26, and 10×14 vs 11×13 for 48. When a source board is narrow, teacher checks placement and may use nonrectangular shapes within the grid. A correct numerical perimeter alone cannot certify that a student actually drew two distinct, closed, axis-aligned polygons.

Original teacher lesson synthesis asks why the same fixed number of interconnected paperclips can be bent into different shapes without changing length. Students should contrast boundary length with enclosed area and explain multiple strategies (count segments, sum sides, double paired sides). Original shape drawings are accessed by a link to the 2021 PDF; all graphic pixels, publisher logos, and gated Cool-down tasks remain outside the Edulytics authored content. No runtime tests, CI, Stage D, publication or academic approval were performed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Perimeter sum
KeyConcepts.Definition: Sum of lengths along the entire closed outer boundary.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Count every horizontal or vertical dot-to-dot interval exactly once.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equal-perimeter shapes
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different shapes have the same total boundary length.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Equal perimeter does not require the same area or same outline.
KeyConcepts.Example: Original source A, G and H all have perimeter 18 grid units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Concave perimeter
KeyConcepts.Definition: Inward dents are part of the boundary.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Include every notch segment for source A, F, I, J.
KeyConcepts.Example: Original source F has a 22-unit outline with an indentation.

KeyConcepts.Title: Dot-grid unit consistency
KeyConcepts.Definition: A horizontal or vertical nearest-neighbor dot interval is one grid unit.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not count a diagonal as one grid unit.
KeyConcepts.Example: Teacher requires only horizontal and vertical drawing sides in Activity 2.

KeyConcepts.Title: Constructing multiple answers
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different closed shapes can satisfy one target total perimeter.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Provide two distinct feasible axis-aligned shapes, explain lengths, teacher approves.

WorkedExamples.Title: Same perimeter different shape A and G
WorkedExamples.Question: How can source shapes A and G have the same perimeter?
WorkedExamples.Method: Count intervals around each original shape.
Steps: Source A outer step path has total 18 unit intervals.
Source G is a 7-by-2 rectangle, so 7+2+7+2=18.
Their enclosed regions are not congruent.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A and G each have 18 grid units.
WorkedExamples.Check: Original teacher notes A/G share perimeter; source PDF vector edges independently checked.

WorkedExamples.Title: All original source perimeter families
WorkedExamples.Question: Which other shape has the same perimeter as source F?
WorkedExamples.Method: Measure each source outline, including indentations.
WorkedExamples.Check: F and J are noncongruent concave polygons.

WorkedExamples.Title: Construct two shapes with perimeter 12
WorkedExamples.Question: Draw two different axis-aligned shapes with 12-grid-unit perimeter.
Steps: Teacher checks drawings fit grid, are closed and nonidentical.
WorkedExamples.Check: A number alone is not proof the shapes exist on the actual board.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat two figures that enclose a similar area as having the same perimeter.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Boundary length depends on edge lengths and indentations, not area.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Stop at the rectangular bounding box when source F or J is indented.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Trace the actual concave edge segments.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use a diagonal step as one unit on the original drawing board.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A diagonal across a square grid cell is longer than a horizontal or vertical unit.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use only grid-aligned horizontal/vertical edges for original open drawings.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume any proposed rectangle fits on the original dot grid.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A 23-long rectangle needs at least 23 source grid intervals.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Choose compact feasible side lengths or other valid shapes.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Automatically mark all closed drawings correct from the perimeter number only.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Teacher must evaluate boundary, distinctness, geometry and explanation.

SummaryPoints: Warm-up true/false sequence: false, true, false, true; base sum 396.
Equal perimeter families: A/G/H, B/E, C/D/I, F/J.
Activity 2: two different horizontal/vertical grid drawings per target 12,26,48; partner chooses another.
Original source diagrams linked only, publisher Cool-down gated; Stage D/tests/academic approval deferred.
